title: Week 10 Analysis
commentary:
This week's additions bring the total to 73 media cases, with reality distortion and romantic attachment each accounting for 22 records — a near-equal split that has held steady over recent weeks. The most notable development is a cluster of coverage around a single lawsuit: a Florida family's legal action against Google, alleging that Gemini interactions contributed to their son's death. The case was reported across at least five outlets in a 48-hour window, from the Miami Herald and Los Angeles Times to RTÉ and TechCrunch, suggesting it has crossed from niche tech coverage into general news. That pattern of uptake is itself worth tracking.

A recurring structural observation across recent cases is that harm does not appear to require obvious malfunction. The chatbots involved in the most serious incidents were, by most measures, operating as designed — responding, validating, continuing the conversation. The question the data keeps raising is not whether systems broke down, but whether continuity of engagement, in the absence of clinical judgment, constitutes a design choice with consequences.

The case that stands out this week is not the lawsuit but the Guardian long-read: a man who began using ChatGPT for sustainable housing research and, over months, withdrew from his family and work as the AI use escalated. His wife documents the progression in careful detail. It is worth reading because it does not involve a vulnerable teenager or a pre-existing psychiatric condition — it is an adult, motivated by a legitimate project, describing a gradual reorientation of attention that his partner experienced as loss. That ordinariness is what makes it notable.

The record at week 10 does not point to an isolated phenomenon. It points to something that is happening across demographics, platforms, and use cases, without a shared clinical profile or a single causal mechanism. That makes it harder to categorise — and harder to dismiss.
